newsitem.title: USA: Grain exports 1.5 mln T short of goal in W. Canada.
newsitem.headline: Grain exports 1.5 mln T short of goal in W. Canada.

text.p: Severe winter weather has interrupted the smooth flow of grain to Canada's western ports, putting exports 1.5 million tonnes behind in January, officials with the Canadian Wheat Board said.
More delays are expected in February and March as shippers work to catch up after rail shipments were impeded by snow-covered tracks, avalanches and frigid cold.
"It could take a few months to get back to normal," said Brian Stacey, a Canadian Wheat Board spokesman.
"I don't think there is any question there will be a rollout (moving loadings back) from February to March, a fairly substantial one."

Severe cold impedes the effectiveness of air brakes on trains, forcing railroads to reduce train speeds and the length of trains, said railroad officals. This means more trains are running on the same tracks and more engines are needed to deliver the same amount of grain.

No foreign buyers have cancelled purchases yet, but there is a huge lineup of grain vessels at Vancouver and Prince Rupert ports and some have been waiting up to 30 days to load, versus a normal wait of 10 days or less, said Stacey.
In addition to slow rail shipments, abundant rain and snow at Vancouver have slowed vessel loadings.
"We've had unheard-of snowfall on the coast," said Bruce Clunie, a senior trader at X-Can Grain. "The rail movement slowed to a crawl."
Clunie said it would be "highly optimistic" to believe the delays can be corrected by the end of March.
"It has not been a good winter, weather-wise," said Steve Morris, manager of public affairs for the Canadian Pacific Railway, a unit of Canadian Pacific Ltd.

Railroads have been hampered by frigid cold, snow-covered tracks, and avalanches in central British Columbia, said Morris. He estimated it will take at least four weeks before railroad operations return to normal.
